Title: The Strategic Imperative of Acquiring Greenland: Unlocking Untapped Potential for the United States

Introduction

Over the past few years, the idea of the United States acquiring Greenland has resurfaced as a topic of discussion. While the notion might seem extraordinary, it is not without historical precedence - President Harry S. Truman unsuccessfully attempted to purchase Greenland back in 1946. Amid new global and geopolitical realities, the arguments in favor of acquiring the world's largest island now hold more weight than ever before. In this essay, I will illustrate why it is crucial for the United States to actively pursue the acquisition of Greenland from Denmark, emphasizing the strategic advantages, resource opportunities, and geopolitical benefits of securing this territory.

Strategic Advantages

Acquiring Greenland would significantly enhance United States strategic interests in the Arctic region. As climate change leads to the melting of polar ice caps, new Arctic shipping routes are becoming accessible, offering a shorter and more direct route connecting Asia, Europe, and North America. Control over Greenland would provide the United States with a base to monitor and potentially influence the use of these new shipping routes. Consequently, securing commercial and military control over this vital transportation corridor would further strengthen America's role as a primary global power.

Moreover, Greenland's strategic location provides the United States with a critical foothold in its northern approach to protecting North American airspace – a mission that is growing in importance as Russia continues to expand its military presence in the Arctic. The Thule Air Base – already under U.S. control – would be further reinforced and expanded as part of the acquisition, enhancing America's ability to address any potential threats from unfriendly foreign powers. Additionally, the acquisition of Greenland would afford the United States with a unique opportunity to establish a more comprehensive ballistic missile defense system, further insulating the nation from any potential aggression.

Resource Opportunities

Greenland's vast untapped resources present enormous economic potential that the United States can ill afford to ignore. Geological surveys indicate that beneath its ice sheet, Greenland likely contains substantial deposits of rare earth metals, uranium, iron ore, and other valuable minerals. Access to these resources would bolster the United States' efforts to reduce its dependence on foreign-controlled supply chains and secure domestic sources of essential strategic minerals. This would not only have immense economic benefits, but also impede China's current efforts to establish a monopoly on rare earth metal production – a development that could leave the United States at a severe strategic disadvantage.

Moreover, Greenland holds the potential of becoming a significant oil and gas producer as the Arctic opens up due to climate change. Securing access to these energy sources would allow the United States to continue its recent strides in becoming an energy-independent nation, as well as reshape the global oil and gas landscape, bolstering U.S. influence and geopolitical power.

Geopolitical Benefits

Finally, the acquisition of Greenland creates a substantial opportunity for the United States to deepen its influence in the Arctic. The Arctic region is growing in importance as global powers – notably Russia and China – seek to establish a strong presence in the area, thereby posing potential threats to the United States' security, as well as the stability and environmental wellbeing of the region. Acquiring Greenland puts the U.S. in a stronger position to counterbalance any expansionist aspirations displayed by these foreign powers and uphold the sovereignty of smaller Arctic countries.

Furthermore, a closer partnership between Greenland and the United States promises the mutually beneficial potential for sustainable economic development. Greenland's population currently faces high unemployment rates and limited fiscal resources. With U.S. investment and economic cooperation, Greenland could develop into a stronger regional player and reliable ally in international forums, thereby reinforcing American foreign policy objectives.

Conclusion

The strategic advantages, resource opportunities, and geopolitical benefits presented by the acquisition of Greenland are all clear and compelling reasons for the United States to actively pursue the matter with Denmark. While the proposition may seem unconventional, it would not be the first time the U.S. has successfully acquired foreign territory to further its interests – the Louisiana Purchase and the acquisition of Alaska both proved to be far-sighted and transformative decisions in American history. As the global stage shifts, it is crucial for the United States to take proactive measures to secure its strategic interests, and it is in this spirit that acquiring Greenland should be accorded the utmost priority.

Why Some U.S. Strategists Have Talked About “Acquiring” Greenland

(Strategic military positioning, natural‑resource access, and national‑security calculations)

> Note: The United States has never formally pursued a legal claim to Greenland, and any discussion of “acquisition” is speculative and highly controversial. The points below outline the strategic logic that has been cited by analysts and policymakers when the idea is raised, not a recommendation or endorsement of any particular policy.

1. Strategic Military Positioning

Aspect Why Greenland Matters How It Would Serve U.S. Interests
Arctic Gate‑way Greenland sits at the crossroads of the Arctic Ocean, the North Atlantic, and the North Pacific (via the Bering Strait). It is the most northerly point of the U.S. sphere of influence in the Western Hemisphere. Provides a forward base for monitoring and controlling emerging Arctic sea‑lane traffic, including the Northern Sea Route and Northeast Passage that may become viable as ice recedes.
Early‑warning & Ballistic‑missile Defense The island’s high latitude offers line‑of‑sight to Russian missile launches from the Kola Peninsula and to potential Chinese long‑range assets operating in the Arctic. A U.S. radar or missile‑defense site in Greenland could integrate into the Ballistic Missile Defense System (e.g., THAAD, Aegis Ashore) and give earlier detection of inbound threats, extending the defensive “kill‑zone” before they reach the continental United States.
Air‑refueling & Fighter/Reconnaissance Staging Existing U.S. installations (e.g., Thule Air Base) already support long‑range air patrols. The island’s runways can accommodate heavy cargo and surveillance aircraft. Adding or expanding bases would allow U.S. Air Force Strategic Air Command (or its modern equivalents) to project power across the North Atlantic, conduct AEW&C (Airborne Early Warning & Control), and sustain Arctic patrols without requiring overflight of allied or foreign sovereign airspace.
Submarine Warfare The deep, ice‑covered waters off Greenland are ideal for anti‑submarine warfare (ASW) training and for monitoring Russian strategic submarines that operate from the Kola Fleet. A U.S. ASW hub could deploy P‑3/ P‑8 Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft and surface vessels to track Russian SSBNs (ballistic‑missile submarines) that use the Arctic as a “safe haven.”
Logistical Redundancy Current U.S. Arctic infrastructure (Alaska, Canada, Iceland) is spread thin. Greenland would add a “third leg” of logistics support. In a crisis (e.g., conflict in Europe, a North‑Atlantic confrontation, or a severe weather event) the U.S. would have an alternative staging ground for troops, equipment, and humanitarian aid.

What Would an “Acquisition” Enable?

  1. Unrestricted Operational Control – Full U.S. sovereignty would eliminate diplomatic constraints (e.g., need for Danish approval for runway extensions, missile‑defense installations, or intelligence‑gathering activities).
  2. Legal Authority for Permanent Bases – The United States could convert the current “lease” (the 1951 U.S.–Denmark defense agreement) into outright ownership, making long‑term investment in hardened facilities, underground bunkers, and renewable‑energy power grids more politically palatable at home.
  3. Strategic Depth – If the U.S. were to lose access to European bases in a future crisis (e.g., a severe escalation with Russia), Greenland would provide a fallback position with existing infrastructure and a low population base that is easier to secure.

2. Access to Natural Resources

Resource Current Estimates & Trends Strategic Value to the United States
Rare‑Earth Elements (REE) & Critical Minerals Greenland’s Kvanefjeld and Narsaq zones contain high concentrations of rare earths (especially neodymium, praseodymium, and dysprosium), as well as uranium, zirconium, and thorium. The US Geological Survey (USGS) estimates that Greenland could host 10‑15% of the world’s REE reserves. Reduces U.S. dependence on China for REEs that are essential for electric‑vehicle motors, high‑performance magnets, aerospace components, and advanced weapons systems.
Petroleum & Natural Gas The West Greenland offshore basins (e.g., the Northeast Greenland Sea, Baffin Bay) have shown promising hydrocarbon signatures. Estimates vary, but some models suggest several billions of barrels of oil equivalent in recoverable reserves. Provides a domestic (or near‑domestic) source of energy, diversifying the supply chain and potentially feeding a strategic petroleum reserve situated in the Arctic.
Lithium & Battery Metals Geochemical surveys indicate lithium‑bearing pegmatites in the Ilulissat area and elsewhere. As the U.S. pushes for a domestic battery supply chain, Greenland could become a supplemental source. Enhances the U.S. capacity to produce batteries for electric vehicles, grid storage, and portable power for forward operating bases.
Fishery Resources The waters around Greenland are among the world’s most productive for cod, haddock, shrimp, and crab. Annual catches run into hundreds of thousands of tons. Guarantees U.S. access to a secure, high‑value protein source for both civilian markets and military rations, and offers a lucrative export commodity.
Renewable Energy (Hydro, Wind, Geothermal) Greenland’s glaciers and rivers yield high‑potential hydroelectric sites. Its wind corridors (especially on the eastern coast) are among the strongest on the planet. Could power U.S. Arctic bases with clean energy, reducing logistics costs for fuel resupply and showcasing U.S. commitment to climate‑friendly defense infrastructure.

Why “Acquisition” Might Be Seen as Advantageous

  • Control Over Licensing & Revenue – Full ownership would allow the U.S. government (or authorized private partners) to grant extraction permits, collect royalties, and direct the development of resource projects in line with national security priorities.
  • Supply‑Chain Security – By integrating Greenland’s critical‑mineral production into U.S. supply‑chain legislation (e.g., the Defense Production Act), the United States can protect key defense industries from foreign export bans or market disruptions.
  • Strategic Stockpiling – The government could establish stockpiles of REEs, lithium, and rare metals directly on Greenland’s coast, reducing transport vulnerabilities.
  • Technology Demonstration Site – Greenland’s harsh environment serves as a real‑world testbed for cold‑climate mining, autonomous drilling, and remote‑operations technologies that the Pentagon and private sector could later apply in other high‑latitude theaters (e.g., Alaska, Siberia).

3. Enhancing National‑Security Interests

(a) Geopolitical Competition in the Arctic

Trend Implication for U.S. Security
Russia’s Arctic Militarization – Russia has reopened Soviet‑era bases (e.g., Barents Sea), deployed Icebreaker warships, and added new airfields in the Arctic. The United States must maintain a counter‑presence to deter Russian attempts to dominate the region and to protect NATO’s northern flank.
China’s “Polar Silk Road” – China has invested in Greenlandic mining, financed research stations, and signed “strategic partnership” deals with Denmark. A U.S. sovereign foothold would limit Chinese economic leverage and block potential dual‑use infrastructure that could be repurposed for intelligence gathering or logistics.
Climate‑change‑enabled Sea Lanes – By mid‑century the Arctic could see up to 2,000 nautical miles of seasonally ice‑free routes, shortening Europe‑Asia shipping times. Controlling Greenland would give the U.S. a say in how those routes are regulated, ensuring freedom of navigation (FON) and protecting commercial shipping from coercive claims.

(b) Early‑Warning and Intelligence

  • Space‑based Sensors – Greenland’s high latitude is ideal for ground‑based optical and radar sensors that augment satellite surveillance (e.g., tracking hypersonic glide vehicles, low‑orbit satellites, and high‑altitude balloons).
  • Signals‑Intelligence (SIGINT) – A U.S. listening post could intercept communications from Arctic naval vessels, Russian early‑warning radars, and Chinese research aircraft—information that is currently difficult to gather from the continental U.S. or Europe.

(c) Resilience of Critical Infrastructure

  • Redundant Power & Communication Nodes – By placing fiber‑optic submarine cables that connect Europe, the U.S., and Asia via Greenland, the United States would gain an additional, politically secure route for data traffic, mitigating vulnerabilities in the Atlantic‑Pacific fiber network.
  • Disaster‑Response Hub – In the event of a large‑scale climate disaster (e.g., massive ice‑sheet collapse, a pandemic, or a cyber‑attack on coastal infrastructure), Greenland could serve as a staging area for humanitarian aid or evacuation operations for the North Atlantic region.

(d) Domestic Political & Economic Benefits

  • Job Creation – Development of mining, construction, and support services would generate employment both for Greenlandic residents and for U.S. contractors, providing a political “win” for Congress and for the administration.
  • Strategic Alliances – While acquisition would be controversial, the United States could leverage the move to renegotiate the U.S.–Denmark defense agreement with more favorable terms (e.g., increased funding for Arctic research, joint climate‑resilience projects).

4. Potential Counterarguments & Risks (Why the Idea Remains Controversial)

Concern Explanation
International Law & Sovereignty Greenland is an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark. Any “transfer” would require Denmark’s consent and likely a UN‑Security‑Council process. Forced acquisition would be illegal under the UN Charter and could trigger sanctions.
Diplomatic Fallout An attempt to purchase or annex Greenland could damage U.S. relations with NATO allies (especially Norway and Canada, who also have Arctic interests) and could push neutral or friendly nations toward Russia or China.
Economic Viability The high cost of building, maintaining, and operating Arctic infrastructure (e.g., roads, ports, power) can outweigh the anticipated revenue from resource extraction, especially given market volatility for commodities like oil.
Environmental & Indigenous Rights Greenland’s ecosystems are fragile, and mining activities could threaten glaciers, wildlife, and the livelihoods of the Inuit population. International backlash over environmental damage could outweigh strategic gains.
Strategic Overreach Holding a remote, sparsely populated territory could stretch U.S. defense resources; the cost of defending Greenland against a determined Russian or Chinese incursion may be high relative to its strategic value.

5. Bottom‑Line Summary

Strategic Dimension Key “Benefits” Cited by Proponents
Military Positioning Forward Arctic base for missile‑defense, surveillance, ASW, and air‑refueling; redundancy for U.S. North‑Atlantic power projection.
Natural Resources Direct access to rare‑earths, lithium, uranium, oil/gas, and abundant fishery stocks; ability to secure critical‑materials supply chains and develop renewable‑energy sites.
National Security Counterbalance Russian and Chinese Arctic ambitions; early‑warning and SIGINT capabilities; control over emerging Arctic sea‑lane routes; resilient logistical hub for crisis response.
Geopolitical Leverage Strengthened negotiating position with Denmark and NATO; a tangible demonstration of U.S. commitment to Arctic security and to protecting “freedom of navigation.”

Caveat: While these points outline why some analysts view Greenland as a strategically attractive asset, the reality of acquiring sovereign territory involves complex legal, diplomatic, environmental, and fiscal considerations. Any policy move would have to reconcile the strategic upside with the substantial risks and international norms that govern state behavior.

The Strategic Imperative: Why the United States Should Acquire Greenland from Denmark

Greenland, the world's largest island, has long been a subject of intrigue and strategic interest due to its vast resources, geopolitical significance, and environmental uniqueness. While it has been a self-governing territory within the Kingdom of Denmark since 1979, the United States should actively pursue its acquisition. This bold move would not only cement the U.S. as a global leader in the Arctic but also enhance national security, tap into immense natural resources, and establish a stronghold in a region of growing geopolitical importance.

Strategic Advantages

Acquiring Greenland would provide the United States with numerous strategic advantages. Firstly, Greenland's location is crucial for military and defense purposes. Its proximity to the North Pole and its strategic position between North America, Europe, and the Arctic Circle make it an ideal location for military bases and surveillance operations. The Thule Air Base, already a U.S. Air Force facility, underscores the strategic importance of Greenland in missile defense and early warning systems.

Moreover, the Arctic is increasingly becoming a focal point for global military and economic interests. Russia, China, and other nations are expanding their presence in the region, seeking to exploit its resources and potentially militarize the area. By securing Greenland, the United States would enhance its ability to counterbalance these influences, ensuring that the Arctic remains a stable and peaceful zone.

Resource Opportunities

Greenland is rich in natural resources, including minerals, hydrocarbons, and freshwater. The island is believed to hold significant deposits of rare earth metals, which are critical for modern technologies such as smartphones, electric vehicles, and renewable energy systems. Currently, China dominates the global market for rare earth metals. Owning Greenland would give the United States direct access to these valuable resources, reducing dependence on foreign suppliers and enhancing economic security.

Additionally, Greenland's large reserves of oil and natural gas, coupled with its abundant freshwater resources, present substantial economic opportunities. The acquisition of Greenland would allow the U.S. to diversify its energy sources, potentially leading to lower energy costs and reduced emissions through the development of green energy projects.

Geopolitical Benefits

From a geopolitical standpoint, acquiring Greenland would solidify the United States' position as a key player in Arctic affairs. It would provide a platform to promote international cooperation in the region, addressing issues such as climate change, environmental conservation, and sustainable development. The U.S. could lead efforts to create a robust framework for Arctic governance, ensuring that the region's resources are managed responsibly and its ecosystems protected.

Furthermore, Greenland's acquisition could be a symbol of ongoing transatlantic cooperation. By collaborating with Denmark and the Greenlandic government, the U.S. could model a respectful and mutually beneficial territorial transition. This approach could strengthen ties between the U.S., Europe, and the broader international community, reinforcing a commitment to shared goals and democratic values.

Environmental Stewardship

Greenland's unique environmental landscape also offers a significant opportunity for scientific research and sustainability initiatives. The island is a critical site for studying climate change, given its rapidly melting ice sheet. By acquiring Greenland, the U.S. could invest in advanced climate research, providing valuable insights into global warming and its impacts. This scientific endeavor could contribute to global efforts to mitigate climate change and adapt to its effects.

Additionally, Greenland's pristine wilderness areas could be preserved as natural reserves, promoting ecotourism and conservation. The U.S. has a strong tradition of environmental protection, and acquiring Greenland would present an opportunity to extend these principles to the Arctic, ensuring that its delicate ecosystems are safeguarded for future generations.

Economic and Social Development

Finally, the acquisition of Greenland could bring substantial economic and social benefits to its inhabitants. With a population of around 56,000, Greenland faces unique challenges and opportunities. The U.S. could invest in infrastructure development, education, and healthcare, improving the lives of Greenlanders and fostering economic growth. This investment would not only benefit the local population but also create new economic ties and opportunities for both the U.S. and Greenland.

Conclusion

The acquisition of Greenland by the United States is a forward-thinking and strategic move that would yield tremendous benefits across various domains. It would enhance national security, provide access to valuable resources, strengthen geopolitical standing, promote environmental stewardship, and foster economic and social development. The U.S. has a historical precedent of strategic acquisitions, such as the Louisiana Purchase and the Alaska Purchase, which have yielded long-term benefits. Acquiring Greenland would be a similarly visionary and beneficial decision, securing the U.S.'s position as a leader in the Arctic and the global stage. The time to act is now.

The Case for American Acquisition of Greenland: A Strategic Imperative for the Twenty-First Century

Introduction

In 1867, Secretary of State William Seward negotiated the purchase of Alaska from Russia for $7.2 million—a deal mocked at the time as "Seward's Folly." Today, Alaska stands as one of the most strategically and economically valuable territories in American history. The United States now faces a comparable opportunity: the acquisition of Greenland, the world's largest island, through good-faith negotiation with Denmark and the Greenlandic people. Far from being a fanciful real estate venture, the pursuit of Greenland represents sound strategic foresight. The convergence of Arctic geopolitics, critical mineral scarcity, and intensifying great-power competition makes Greenland's acquisition one of the most consequential opportunities available to American policymakers—one that could benefit the United States, Denmark, and Greenlanders alike if pursued through lawful, consensual means.

Strategic and Military Advantages

Greenland's geographic position is, quite simply, irreplaceable. Sitting astride the shortest air routes between North America and Europe and dominating the maritime approaches to the North Atlantic, the island has been central to American defense planning since World War II. The United States already operates Pituffik Space Base (formerly Thule Air Base) in northwestern Greenland, a critical node in America's ballistic missile early-warning system and space surveillance network. Yet operating a single base under a defense agreement is a far cry from possessing the strategic depth that full integration of the territory would provide.

Greenland anchors the famous GIUK gap—the Greenland-Iceland-United Kingdom corridor through which Russian submarines must pass to reach the open Atlantic. As Russia rebuilds its Northern Fleet and militarizes its Arctic coastline with refurbished Soviet-era bases, control of this chokepoint becomes paramount. An American Greenland would allow for expanded anti-submarine warfare infrastructure, additional radar and sensor installations, and forward basing for naval and air assets, dramatically strengthening NATO's northern flank.

Moreover, as climate change opens the Arctic to year-round navigation, the region is transforming from a frozen buffer into a contested maritime frontier. The United States currently lags badly in Arctic capability—possessing a handful of aging icebreakers compared to Russia's fleet of more than forty. Sovereign control over Greenland's deep-water ports and extensive coastline would give the United States the territorial foundation necessary to become a genuine Arctic power rather than a peripheral observer.

Resource Opportunities

Beneath Greenland's ice sheet and along its exposed coastal margins lies one of the planet's great untapped storehouses of natural wealth. The strategic significance of these resources cannot be overstated.

Rare earth elements. Greenland holds some of the world's largest known deposits of rare earth minerals—the indispensable inputs for semiconductors, electric vehicle motors, wind turbines, precision-guided munitions, and virtually every advanced technology of the modern era. China currently controls roughly 70 percent of global rare earth mining and nearly 90 percent of processing capacity, a stranglehold it has repeatedly signaled willingness to weaponize. American development of Greenlandic deposits at sites like Kvanefjeld and Kringlerne could break this dependency, securing supply chains essential to both national defense and the clean energy transition.

Critical and precious minerals. Beyond rare earths, Greenland contains significant deposits of uranium, zinc, copper, nickel, graphite, titanium, and gold. These are precisely the materials over which the next century's industrial competition will be waged.

Energy resources. The U.S. Geological Survey has estimated that the waters off Greenland may hold tens of billions of barrels of oil and vast natural gas reserves. Even if developed cautiously, these reserves represent a strategic hedge of enormous value.

Fisheries and fresh water. Greenland's waters support some of the richest fisheries in the North Atlantic, and its ice sheet contains roughly 7 percent of the world's fresh water—a resource whose value will only appreciate in a warming, water-stressed world.

Critically, American capital, technology, and environmental engineering expertise could develop these resources responsibly in ways that Greenland's tiny population of 57,000 and modest government budget simply cannot achieve alone.

Geopolitical Benefits

The acquisition of Greenland must be understood in the context of accelerating great-power competition in the Arctic. China has declared itself a "near-Arctic state," sought to purchase abandoned military installations in Greenland, attempted to finance Greenlandic airports, and pursued mining concessions across the island. These are not commercial ventures undertaken for their own sake; they are pieces of a deliberate strategy to establish a "Polar Silk Road" and gain a foothold in the Western Hemisphere. Denmark has been forced to repeatedly intervene to block Chinese acquisitions—a defensive posture that cannot be sustained indefinitely against a determined superpower with vastly deeper pockets.

American acquisition would permanently foreclose this threat. It would deny Beijing and Moscow any opening in the North Atlantic, consolidate the Western Hemisphere under the security umbrella envisioned by the Monroe Doctrine, and position the United States to shape the rules governing newly opening Arctic shipping lanes—routes that could cut transit times between Asia and Europe by 40 percent and reshape global commerce.

There is also a compelling argument from alliance management. Denmark, a nation of six million people, bears responsibility for defending a landmass three times the size of Texas—a burden it candidly cannot meet. Copenhagen spends heavily to subsidize Greenland's government (roughly $500–600 million annually) while lacking the military capacity to secure it. A negotiated transfer, accompanied by generous compensation and continued Danish commercial access, would relieve Denmark of an unsustainable obligation while strengthening the NATO alliance as a whole.

A Genuine Partnership with Greenlanders

Any acquisition worth pursuing must be one that Greenlanders themselves choose. This is not merely a moral requirement but a practical one—and here the American offer is genuinely attractive. Greenland's economy depends overwhelmingly on fishing and Danish subsidies. Its people face limited economic opportunity, inadequate infrastructure, and isolation from global markets. Association with the United States—whether as a territory with a path to statehood, a commonwealth arrangement, or a compact of free association—could bring transformative investment: modern hospitals, universities, broadband, airports, and the capital to develop resources on terms favorable to local communities. Greenlanders could be guaranteed protections for Inuit language, culture, and land rights stronger than any they currently enjoy, alongside per-capita prosperity that subsidized dependence on Copenhagen can never deliver. The United States should make an offer so generous, so respectful of self-determination, that Greenlanders see it as their opportunity, not America's conquest.

Answering the Objections

Critics call the idea absurd, but history says otherwise. The United States purchased Louisiana from France, Alaska from Russia, and—most pertinently—the Virgin Islands from Denmark itself in 1917 for $25 million. The Truman administration secretly offered Denmark $100 million in gold for Greenland in 1946, recognizing precisely the strategic logic outlined here. Territorial acquisition through negotiated purchase is not imperialism; it is statecraft with deep precedent in both American and Danish history.

Others object to the cost. But weigh the price—even hundreds of billions of dollars—against the value: trillions in mineral wealth, permanent strategic security in the Arctic, and the foreclosure of Chinese and Russian ambitions in the Western Hemisphere. Few investments in American history would offer comparable returns.

Conclusion

Great nations are defined by their ability to recognize historic opportunities and act upon them. The Louisiana Purchase doubled the republic; the Alaska Purchase secured its Pacific and Arctic frontiers. Greenland represents the twenty-first century's equivalent—a chance to secure America's northern approaches, break adversarial control of critical minerals, dominate the emerging Arctic theater, and extend prosperity to a people whose potential has long been constrained. The United States should open serious, respectful negotiations with Copenhagen and Nuuk, backed by an offer of historic generosity. Future generations will judge whether this era's leaders possessed Seward's vision—or whether they let "Greenland's Folly" become the opportunity America was too timid to seize.

The Strategic Imperative: Why the United States Must Acquire Greenland

In an era of shifting global power dynamics, resource scarcity, and heightened geopolitical competition, the United States must seize the opportunity to secure Greenland, a vast and strategically situated territory currently under Danish sovereignty. Acquiring Greenland would provide the U.S. with unparalleled strategic advantages, unlock immense resource opportunities, and solidify its position as a dominant global power. This move is not merely an optional policy consideration but a necessary step to safeguard American interests in the 21st century and beyond.

Strategic Advantages

Greenland’s geographic location makes it a linchpin for global security and a strategic asset for the United States. Situated between the North Atlantic and Arctic oceans, Greenland serves as a natural gateway to the Arctic, a region increasingly crucial for its untapped resources and emerging shipping routes. As climate change accelerates the melting of polar ice, the Arctic is becoming more accessible, opening new avenues for trade, energy exploration, and military operations. By acquiring Greenland, the U.S. would gain a commanding presence in this vital region, countering the growing influence of rivals such as Russia and China.

Russia has already invested heavily in militarizing the Arctic, building new bases and deploying advanced weaponry to project power in the region. China, too, has declared itself a "near-Arctic state" and is actively pursuing partnerships and infrastructure projects to expand its influence. Greenland’s acquisition would allow the U.S. to establish military bases, enhance surveillance capabilities, and secure its northern frontier. The Thule Air Base, already operated by the U.S. in Greenland, could be expanded into a larger hub for Arctic operations, ensuring American dominance in this increasingly contested theater.

Resource Opportunities

Greenland is not just a strategic location; it is a treasure trove of natural resources. The island is estimated to hold vast reserves of rare earth elements, critical minerals, and hydrocarbons essential for modern technology, renewable energy, and national defense. Rare earth elements, in particular, are indispensable for manufacturing semiconductors, electric vehicles, wind turbines, and advanced weaponry. Currently, China dominates the global supply chain for these materials, giving it significant leverage over the U.S. and its allies. Acquiring Greenland would enable the U.S. to break this dependency and establish a secure, domestic supply of critical resources.

In addition to minerals, Greenland’s untapped oil and gas reserves could bolster American energy independence. While global efforts to transition to renewable energy are underway, fossil fuels will remain a cornerstone of the global economy for decades. Access to Greenland’s energy resources would strengthen the U.S. economy, reduce reliance on volatile foreign markets, and enhance national security.

Geopolitical Benefits

Securing Greenland would also yield significant geopolitical advantages. The acquisition would reinforce America’s commitment to its allies in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) by providing a forward base for collective defense. It would also send a clear message to adversaries that the U.S. is prepared to take bold steps to protect its interests and maintain global stability.

Moreover, Greenland’s acquisition would strengthen the U.S.-Denmark relationship. Denmark, while currently the sovereign power over Greenland, faces the challenge of managing a sparsely populated, resource-rich territory far from its shores. By transferring Greenland to the U.S., Denmark could focus on its European priorities while benefiting from enhanced security and economic cooperation with a trusted ally. The U.S. could also negotiate a favorable deal that ensures Denmark’s continued partnership and goodwill.

Critics may argue that acquiring Greenland is politically controversial or economically burdensome. However, the long-term benefits far outweigh the short-term costs. Greenland’s population of approximately 56,000 would require significant investment in infrastructure, healthcare, and education, but this presents an opportunity for the U.S. to demonstrate its capacity for nation-building and its commitment to inclusive growth. Furthermore, the economic returns from Greenland’s resources and strategic value would quickly offset initial expenditures.

Conclusion

The acquisition of Greenland is not a matter of imperial ambition but a strategic necessity. In an increasingly competitive and resource-constrained world, the United States must act decisively to secure its future. Greenland offers unparalleled strategic advantages, vast resource opportunities, and significant geopolitical benefits that align with American interests. By pursuing this acquisition, the U.S. can fortify its position in the Arctic, reduce dependence on foreign rivals, and ensure its continued leadership on the global stage. The time to act is now; Greenland is the key to America’s long-term security and prosperity.

1. Strategic Military Positioning

Greenland’s location in the Arctic affords the U.S. critical advantages in global defense and power projection:

  • Thule Air Base: The U.S. already operates Thule Air Base (now Pituffik Space Base), one of its northernmost military installations, which provides early missile warning capabilities, space surveillance, and ballistic missile defense against potential threats from Russia or China.

  • Countering Foreign Influence: Denmark (Greenland’s sovereign) has faced pressure from Chinese investment in Greenland’s infrastructure (e.g., airports). U.S. ownership would prevent Beijing or Moscow from gaining economic or military footholds.

2. Access to Natural Resources

Greenland is believed to hold vast untapped reserves of critical minerals and energy supplies:

  • Rare Earth Elements (REEs): Greenland has some of the world’s largest deposits of rare earths (essential for advanced tech, military hardware, and renewable energy), reducing U.S. dependence on Chinese supply chains (China controls ~80% of global REE production).
  • Hydrocarbons: Offshore oil and gas reserves could bolster U.S. energy security, though environmental concerns have limited exploration.
  • Freshwater & Fisheries: Greenland’s ice sheet contains ~10% of the world’s freshwater, while its waters are rich in fish stocks—key for long-term resource resilience.

3. Enhanced National Security Interests

  • Climate Change & Geopolitics: Melting Arctic ice increases Greenland’s strategic value for shipping lanes and military mobility. Control would allow the U.S. to monitor and deter Russian submarines and Chinese polar activities.
  • Sovereignty & Legal Control: Direct ownership would allow the U.S. to bypass Danish restrictions on military expansion or resource extraction, ensuring full operational autonomy.
  • Deterrence Against Adversaries: A permanent U.S.-controlled Greenland would serve as a forward base for Arctic operations, strengthening NATO’s northern flank.

Challenges & Counterarguments

Despite these benefits, acquiring Greenland faces obstacles:

  • Danish & Greenlandic Opposition: Greenland has self-rule under Denmark, and polls show most Greenlanders oppose annexation.
  • Economic Costs: Developing Greenland’s infrastructure and economy would require massive investment.
  • Diplomatic Friction: Forcing a purchase could strain U.S.-Danish relations and set a controversial precedent for territorial transactions.

Conclusion

While Greenland’s strategic location, resources, and security value make it a compelling asset, political and logistical hurdles make outright acquisition unlikely in the near term. However, the U.S. may pursue expanded defense agreements, resource partnerships, or economic incentives to secure its interests without full sovereignty.

Greenland occupies a unique position straddling the North Atlantic and the Arctic Ocean. The case for the United States to actively pursue the acquisition of Greenland rests on three interlocking imperatives: strategic dominance of the Arctic, access to a wealth of untapped natural resources, and the ability to shape a responsible, forward‑looking Arctic future.

America's Arctic Imperative: The Strategic Case for Acquiring Greenland

Introduction

When President Harry Truman offered Denmark $100 million for Greenland in 1946, his administration was not engaged in geopolitical fantasy — it was responding to a cold strategic calculus that recognized the island's extraordinary value. When the idea was revived under President Trump and again surfaced in subsequent political discussions, critics dismissed it as eccentric or even imperious. They were wrong to do so. The acquisition of Greenland represents one of the most consequential strategic opportunities available to the United States in the twenty-first century, and a serious, sustained American commitment to pursuing it — through diplomatic negotiation, economic partnership, and genuine engagement with Greenlandic self-determination — deserves far more sober consideration than it typically receives. Geography, resources, geopolitics, and the long arc of history all converge on a single conclusion: securing Greenland would be among the most significant and durable achievements in American strategic history.

This essay argues that the United States should actively and earnestly pursue Greenland's acquisition, not through coercion or imperialism, but through the kind of visionary statecraft that has defined America's greatest territorial moments. The Louisiana Purchase, the Alaska purchase, and the acquisition of the Panama Canal Zone were all derided in their time as wasteful, unnecessary, or hubristic. History vindicated every one of them. Greenland would belong in that company.

Part One: The Arctic Is the New Frontier of Great Power Competition

To understand why Greenland matters, one must first understand what is happening to the Arctic. Climate change, whatever its other consequences, is transforming the High North from a frozen backwater into one of the most contested and consequential regions on Earth. Within decades, summer Arctic sea routes will be reliably navigable, cutting shipping distances between Asia and Europe by thousands of miles. The Northern Sea Route along Russia's coast and the Northwest Passage through Canada's archipelago are already increasingly accessible. A transpolar route passing directly over the Arctic Ocean may eventually become viable as well.

These developments are not hypothetical. The Arctic Council's own scientific assessments project dramatic reductions in sea ice extent. Commercial shipping through Arctic routes is already increasing year over year. The implications for global trade are staggering: a fully operational Arctic shipping corridor would compress transoceanic commerce in ways not seen since the Suez Canal. Nations that control the chokepoints, ports, and surveillance infrastructure along these routes will exercise extraordinary leverage over global commerce.

Greenland sits at the intersection of the Atlantic and Arctic Oceans, occupying a position that military strategists describe with barely concealed reverence. The island's eastern coast faces Europe, its western coast flanks Canada, and its northern tip reaches toward the Arctic Ocean itself. It is the single largest island on Earth, spanning roughly 836,000 square miles — more than three times the size of Texas. Any serious strategic actor examining a map of the emerging Arctic theater would immediately identify Greenland as the keystone. The United States already recognizes this implicitly: Thule Air Base on Greenland's northwest coast has been a critical component of American nuclear deterrence and aerospace warning systems since the Cold War. But a leased installation is a far more fragile asset than sovereign territory.

Russia understands the Arctic's importance with crystalline clarity. Moscow has reopened and expanded Soviet-era Arctic military bases, deployed new icebreakers, planted a flag on the Arctic seabed, and advanced aggressive territorial claims under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. Russia's Arctic strategy is explicit in its official documents: the country views the region as essential to its economic future and national security. China, despite being a non-Arctic state, has declared itself a "near-Arctic power," invested heavily in Arctic research stations, courted Greenlandic officials with infrastructure financing offers, and sought to establish footholds that would give Beijing influence in the region. Chinese state enterprises have repeatedly expressed interest in building airports, mining operations, and ports in Greenland.

The United States, by contrast, has approached the Arctic with a casualness bordering on negligence. America possesses only a handful of operational icebreakers compared to Russia's fleet of more than forty. American Arctic policy has lurched between administrations without consistent strategic vision. This cannot continue. The window for establishing a commanding American position in the Arctic is open now — and it will not remain open indefinitely. Acquiring Greenland would, in a single stroke, give the United States the sovereign Arctic presence necessary to compete effectively with both Russia and China in the defining strategic theater of the coming century.

Part Two: The Resource Wealth Beneath the Ice

Greenland is not merely strategically positioned — it is extraordinarily wealthy. The island sits atop resource deposits that would, if developed, reshape global supply chains and reduce American dependence on rival powers for critical materials.

The United States Geological Survey estimates that Greenland's offshore waters contain approximately 17.5 billion barrels of oil equivalent in undiscovered resources. This would rank among the most significant untapped hydrocarbon reserves in the world. As Arctic ice recedes and extraction technology improves, these deposits will become increasingly accessible. For a United States committed to energy security, the ability to develop these reserves under American sovereign control — rather than watching them developed by European, Chinese, or Russian interests — represents an enormous economic and strategic advantage.

More immediately compelling than hydrocarbons, however, is Greenland's endowment of rare earth elements and critical minerals. This is perhaps the most urgent resource argument for acquisition. Rare earth elements — the seventeen metalite materials essential to electric vehicle motors, wind turbines, advanced electronics, guided munitions, and virtually every modern technology — are currently dominated by Chinese production. China controls approximately 60 percent of global rare earth mining and 85 percent of processing capacity. This dependency represents one of the most serious vulnerabilities in American national security and economic competitiveness. The Defense Department has repeatedly identified rare earth supply chains as a critical strategic weakness.

Greenland's Kvanefjeld deposit in the south of the island is among the largest known rare earth deposits on the planet. The Ilimaussaq complex is estimated to contain millions of tons of rare earth oxides, along with significant uranium deposits. Additional deposits have been identified across the island. Were these resources developed under American sovereign authority, they could fundamentally restructure global rare earth markets, breaking Chinese dominance and providing the United States and its allies with access to materials essential to both military capability and the clean energy transition.

Beyond rare earths, Greenland contains significant deposits of zinc, lead, iron ore, gold, and diamonds. The fisheries in Greenlandic waters are among the most productive in the North Atlantic. As permafrost thaws, previously inaccessible land area may become available for various uses. The aggregate resource wealth represents a generational economic opportunity of the first order.

Critics argue that resource extraction in the Arctic is environmentally destructive and economically uncertain. These are legitimate concerns that deserve serious policy attention. But the question of whether to develop Greenland's resources is distinct from the question of who should control them. If Greenland's resources will be developed regardless — and given the economic pressures on Greenland's small population and the interests of major powers, development will come — then the relevant strategic question is whether American sovereignty reduces or increases the likelihood of responsible stewardship. Given America's regulatory capacity and its ability to structure incentives, this is not an argument against acquisition.

Part Three: Military and Intelligence Advantages

The military case for Greenland is perhaps the most straightforward and least deniable of all the arguments in favor of acquisition. Thule Air Base, currently operated under a 1951 defense agreement with Denmark, is already one of the most important American military installations in the world. It hosts the 21st Space Wing's missile warning systems, space surveillance operations, and serves as a crucial node in America's early warning network for intercontinental ballistic missiles. It is the northernmost American military installation and one of the few facilities from which the United States can monitor Russian Arctic military activity in real time.

But leasing arrangements are strategically inferior to sovereignty in ways that become apparent during moments of pressure. Denmark is a reliable ally and NATO member, and the current arrangement has functioned admirably. Yet the strategic logic of sovereignty is compelling: a nation cannot be forced to renegotiate, impose conditions, or withdraw permission from itself. The American installation at Thule is, under current arrangements, ultimately dependent on Danish goodwill and Danish political stability. Sovereign control eliminates that dependency entirely.

Beyond Thule, American sovereign control over Greenland would enable a comprehensive expansion of military infrastructure across the island's vast coastline. Additional radar installations, submarine detection networks, air defense batteries, and naval facilities could be established at will. The island's position means that American forces based in Greenland could rapidly deploy into the North Atlantic, monitor both the GIUK Gap (the critical chokepoint between Greenland, Iceland, and the United Kingdom through which Russian submarines must pass to reach Atlantic sea lanes) and Arctic Ocean approaches, and project power into the High North in ways currently impossible.

Russian military doctrine explicitly contemplates scenarios in which Arctic sea lanes and resources become theaters of conflict. Chinese naval expansion is relentless. American military planners who have gamed out Arctic scenarios consistently identify Greenland as the critical terrain. Control of that terrain means the difference between defending against adversary moves from a position of strength and scrambling to respond from inferior positions.

The intelligence value of sovereign Greenland extends beyond military hardware. American signals intelligence, human intelligence, and surveillance infrastructure could be expanded dramatically. The island's position allows monitoring of Russian northern fleet movements from Murmansk, tracking of Arctic shipping, and surveillance of Chinese scientific and commercial activities in the region. These capabilities matter enormously in an era of persistent great power competition below the threshold of open conflict.

Part Four: Respecting Greenlandic Self-Determination

Perhaps the most sophisticated objection to American acquisition is that Greenland's people have the right to determine their own political future, and that any American initiative amounts to imperialism. This objection deserves a serious response rather than dismissal, because it actually points toward the most effective and ethical path to acquisition.

Greenland is already a self-governing territory under the Kingdom of Denmark, with its own parliament (the Inatsisartut), its own government, and a 2009 self-governance act that explicitly recognizes the Greenlandic people's right to declare full independence. The population of roughly 56,000, predominantly Greenlandic Inuit, has been exercising increasing autonomy for decades. Many Greenlandic political leaders actively aspire to full independence from Denmark.

This is, counterintuitively, an argument for American engagement rather than against it. Greenland's path to independence is constrained by economics: the island currently receives an annual block grant from Denmark of approximately 3.9 billion Danish kroner (roughly $570 million), which represents a substantial portion of Greenlandic government revenues. Without this subsidy, which would presumably end upon independence, Greenland would struggle to finance its government services and infrastructure. Greenland is too small and too underdeveloped at present to immediately sustain fiscal independence.

An American offer — structured not as conquest but as a genuine partnership or statehood proposal — could resolve this constraint in a way that serves Greenlandic interests. A generous financial arrangement that provides Greenland with resources for infrastructure, education, healthcare, and economic development would give the Greenlandic people something Denmark currently cannot: the means to chart a fully sovereign or co-sovereign course while maintaining economic stability. If Greenlandic citizens were presented with a genuine choice — continue as a subordinate territory of a small European kingdom, pursue fiscal independence with all its difficulties, or enter into a new relationship with the world's largest economy that provides security and economic support while respecting Greenlandic cultural identity — many might find the American option attractive.

The United States should approach this by treating the Greenlandic people as the primary interlocutors, not merely as subjects of a negotiation conducted between Washington and Copenhagen. Any proposal should guarantee the preservation of Greenlandic language, culture, and institutions. It should include robust protections for traditional hunting and fishing practices. It should provide for meaningful Greenlandic representation in any governing arrangement. And it should be accompanied by a serious financial commitment to Greenlandic development that exceeds what Denmark currently provides.

This is not imperialism. Imperial acquisition involves the subordination of a people against their will for the benefit of the acquiring power. What is proposed here is a negotiated arrangement that could substantially improve the material conditions of Greenlandic citizens while serving American strategic interests. These goals are not incompatible. Alaska's negotiated purchase, whatever its complex historical dimensions, produced ultimately beneficial outcomes for governance and development of the territory. The paradigm for Greenland is partnership, not conquest.

Part Five: Managing the Alliance Relationship with Denmark

The most immediate diplomatic obstacle is Denmark itself, which has consistently stated that Greenland is not for sale. This position deserves respect, but it should not be treated as immovable or as the final word on the subject. History is full of positions that shifted when circumstances and incentives changed.

Denmark's resistance is understandable. No nation readily contemplates reducing itself. The Danish-Greenlandic relationship is historically complex and emotionally resonant on both sides. Danish leaders face domestic political pressures that make appearing to "sell" territory deeply uncomfortable. These are real constraints that American diplomacy must navigate with patience and sensitivity rather than bravado.

But it is worth noting that Denmark itself has an ambivalent relationship with the financial burden of Greenland. The annual subsidy represents a significant ongoing commitment for a country of Denmark's size. As climate change makes Greenland more valuable — and potentially more costly to administer as infrastructure needs grow — the calculus may shift. A sufficiently generous American offer that compensates Denmark handsomely, potentially including enhanced security commitments, technological partnerships, and bilateral economic arrangements, could over time make the proposition genuinely attractive to Danish policymakers.

The approach should be sustained and respectful rather than insistent or pressuring. American diplomatic engagement should make clear that the United States views this as a long-term question, that it respects Danish sovereignty, and that it is prepared to compensate Denmark generously and enhance the bilateral relationship in ways that leave Denmark better off. This is not the approach of the bully or the imperialist — it is the approach of a serious statesman who identifies a mutually beneficial arrangement and works patiently toward it.

Furthermore, the framing matters enormously. Rather than a "purchase," which carries colonial overtones, American diplomacy should emphasize partnership, joint stewardship, and shared values. Greenland, Denmark, and the United States are all democratic societies that share fundamental commitments to rule of law, human rights, and open economies. A new arrangement could be framed as deepening that community of democracies rather than as a commercial transaction.

Part Six: The Historical Precedent and the Long View

Every major American territorial expansion was contested in its time by critics who argued it was unnecessary, expensive, or inappropriate. Jefferson's opponents called the Louisiana Purchase unconstitutional. Seward was ridiculed for purchasing "Seward's Folly" — Alaska — a territory that proved to contain enormous oil wealth and strategic significance. The acquisition of California and the Southwest was and remains contested. But the long view of American history vindicates territorial ambition paired with strategic foresight.

The United States is not a static actor in world history. It is a nation that has consistently, when functioning at its best, recognized strategic opportunities and pursued them with a combination of financial resourcefulness and diplomatic creativity. The Louisiana Purchase doubled the nation's size for approximately $15 million — roughly $340 million in today's dollars. Alaska cost $7.2 million. These were extraordinary bargains that shaped everything that followed in American history. The question for contemporary statesmen is whether they possess the same vision as Jefferson and Seward — or whether they are content to manage decline while rival powers position themselves for advantage.

China's growing Arctic ambitions should focus minds. Beijing has explicitly described itself as a near-Arctic power, has sought to finance infrastructure in Greenland, and views the Arctic's opening as an opportunity to establish presence and influence in a region adjacent to the North Atlantic. A Chinese-funded airport in Greenland, a Chinese mining operation, a Chinese research station — individually these may seem modest. Cumulatively and over time, they represent the patient establishment of presence that characterizes Chinese strategic behavior globally. Once established, such presence is difficult to dislodge without the kind of confrontation nobody wants.

The time to act is before that presence is established, not after. The time to negotiate from a position of generosity and goodwill is before competition for Greenland's resources and strategic position intensifies. Every year of inaction is a year in which the strategic landscape evolves in ways less favorable to American interests.

Conclusion: Vision, Not Aggression

The case for pursuing Greenland's acquisition is not a case for aggression, imperialism, or the disregard of international norms. It is a case for vision — for the kind of long-range strategic thinking that has periodically distinguished American statecraft at its finest. The arguments are convergent and mutually reinforcing: Arctic geopolitics demands a permanent American sovereign presence; critical resource security requires access to Greenland's mineral wealth; military strategy necessitates control over one of the world's most important strategic positions; and the Greenlandic people's own aspirations for self-determination create an opening for a genuinely consensual arrangement.

The right approach is patient, respectful, generous, and persistent. It treats the Greenlandic people as full partners with their own legitimate interests. It compensates Denmark fairly and enhances the bilateral relationship. It proposes arrangements that improve the material conditions of everyone involved. And it pursues these goals with the steady confidence of a nation that understands its own strategic interests and is prepared to invest in securing them.

Truman understood this in 1946. Seward understood something similar about Alaska in 1867. The question before American leadership today is whether it possesses the same quality of strategic imagination — and whether it will act before the opportunity closes. The Arctic is opening. The great powers are moving. Greenland is waiting.

America should not hesitate.

The Case for Greenland: Why America Should Pursue the Strategic Acquisition of the World's Largest Island

Introduction

In 1867, the United States purchased Alaska from the Russian Empire for $7.2 million — a transaction widely mocked at the time as "Seward's Folly." Secretary of State William Seward was ridiculed for buying what critics called a frozen wasteland. Within a generation, gold was discovered. Within a century, petroleum. Today, Alaska is one of the most strategically vital and resource-rich territories in American possession.

Greenland represents a remarkably parallel opportunity — one that the United States cannot afford to ignore. At 836,000 square miles, it is the world's largest island, possessing extraordinary mineral wealth, an unrivaled geographic position, and growing strategic significance in an era of intensifying great-power competition. While the acquisition of a sovereign territory involves complex diplomatic, legal, and ethical considerations that must be navigated with care and respect for the Greenlandic people, the pursuit of a mutually beneficial arrangement — whether through purchase, compact, or another creative framework — deserves serious, sustained attention from American policymakers.

This essay argues that the United States should actively and earnestly pursue the acquisition of Greenland, examining the case through four lenses: geographic and military strategy, natural resource security, geopolitical competition, and economic opportunity.

I. Geographic and Military Strategy: Commanding the Arctic Corridor

Greenland occupies one of the most consequential geographic positions on Earth. Situated between the Atlantic and Arctic Oceans, it sits astride increasingly navigable sea routes and provides proximity to both North America and Northern Europe. As climate change continues to reduce Arctic ice coverage — the Northwest Passage could see ice-free summers within decades — the strategic calculus shifts dramatically.

A. The Thule Air Base and Northern Defense

The United States already operates Pituffik Space Base (formerly Thule Air Base) in northwestern Greenland under a 1951 agreement with Denmark. This installation is critical for missile warning systems, space surveillance, and Arctic defense. Yet American access is contingent on the continued goodwill of a foreign government and could, in theory, be revoked or renegotiated under adverse circumstances. Full sovereignty over Greenland would permanently secure this and other potential installations, eliminating a significant vulnerability in America's northern defense architecture.

B. Arctic Shipping Routes

As the Arctic warms, two shipping routes are becoming commercially viable: the Northern Sea Route along Russia's coast and the Northwest Passage through the Canadian Arctic Archipelago. A third route — the Transpolar Sea Route — may become feasible by mid-century, passing directly over the North Pole and near Greenland's northeastern coast. Whoever controls the territories flanking these routes will wield enormous influence over global trade. Greenland gives the United States a commanding position along all three.

C. Submarine Operations and Undersea Warfare

Greenland's deep fjords and the waters surrounding it are strategically significant for submarine operations. The GIUK Gap — the stretch of ocean between Greenland, Iceland, and the United Kingdom — has been a critical chokepoint for naval warfare since World War II. Soviet and now Russian submarines must pass through or near this gap to reach the open Atlantic. Sovereign control of Greenland's territorial waters would significantly enhance American anti-submarine warfare capabilities and reinforce control over this vital corridor.

II. Natural Resource Security: A Vault of Critical Minerals

Greenland is not merely a frozen expanse. Beneath its ice sheet and along its coastlines lies an extraordinary endowment of natural resources, many of which are classified as critical minerals essential for modern technology, renewable energy, and national defense.

A. Rare Earth Elements

Greenland possesses some of the world's largest deposits of rare earth elements (REEs) — a group of 17 minerals essential for manufacturing smartphones, electric vehicles, wind turbines, advanced weaponry, and semiconductors. Currently, China controls approximately 60-70% of global rare earth mining and nearly 90% of rare earth processing. This near-monopoly represents one of the most acute strategic vulnerabilities facing the United States and its allies.

The Kvanefjeld deposit in southern Greenland, along with several other sites, contains substantial REE reserves. Acquiring Greenland would allow the United States to develop these resources domestically, dramatically reducing dependence on Chinese supply chains for materials that are, quite literally, the building blocks of the 21st-century economy.

B. Uranium and Nuclear Fuel

Greenland contains significant uranium deposits. While the island's current government has expressed reservations about uranium mining, sovereign American control would allow for carefully regulated development that balances environmental stewardship with energy security. In an era where nuclear energy is being reconsidered as a clean baseload power source, domestic uranium access is a meaningful strategic advantage.

C. Oil, Gas, and Emerging Energy Resources

The United States Geological Survey has estimated that the waters off northeastern Greenland may contain significant undiscovered petroleum reserves — potentially billions of barrels of oil and trillions of cubic feet of natural gas. As Arctic ice recedes, these resources become increasingly accessible. Additionally, Greenland's potential for hydropower and wind energy is immense, offering opportunities for clean energy development on a continental scale.

D. Freshwater and Cryospheric Resources

Though often overlooked, Greenland's ice sheet contains approximately 10% of the world's freshwater. While large-scale water export remains speculative, in an era of growing global water scarcity, control of this resource represents a long-term strategic asset of incalculable value.

III. Geopolitical Competition: Preventing Strategic Encirclement

The question of Greenland is not merely about what the island contains — it is about who else might seek to control it, and the consequences of American inaction.

A. China's Arctic Ambitions

Beijing has declared itself a "near-Arctic state" — a designation that has no basis in geography but reveals clear strategic intent. China has invested heavily in Arctic research stations, icebreaker vessels, and diplomatic engagement with Arctic nations. In 2018, Chinese state-owned companies attempted to finance airport construction projects in Greenland, an effort that was ultimately blocked by Denmark and the United States. China's interest in Greenland is not humanitarian — it is strategic. Beijing seeks access to rare earth minerals, shipping routes, and geopolitical positioning.

If the United States does not secure Greenland, it risks watching China establish economic footholds — or worse — that could compromise American security interests in the Arctic. The Monroe Doctrine's logic, updated for the 21st century, argues compellingly against allowing a hostile foreign power to gain strategic advantages in the Western Hemisphere's northern reaches.

B. Russia's Arctic Militarization

Russia has been aggressively militarizing its Arctic coastline, reopening Soviet-era bases, deploying advanced air defense systems, and establishing new military commands dedicated to Arctic operations. Russia claims vast portions of the Arctic seabed under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and has planted a titanium flag on the ocean floor beneath the North Pole. American sovereignty over Greenland would counterbalance Russia's growing Arctic presence and ensure that the United States maintains parity — or superiority — in the polar regions.

C. Maintaining the Balance of Power

The Arctic is rapidly becoming the world's next great arena of strategic competition. The nations that establish dominance there will shape the international order for decades. The United States, as the world's preeminent military and economic power, has both the capability and the responsibility to ensure that the Arctic remains a region of stability, openness, and adherence to international norms — rather than a zone of authoritarian expansion.

IV. Economic Opportunity: Development and Prosperity

Beyond military and geopolitical considerations, Greenland presents extraordinary economic development opportunities.

A. Infrastructure and Modernization

Greenland's population of approximately 56,000 currently depends heavily on Danish subsidies, which account for roughly half of the island's government budget. American acquisition — structured as a generous compact that respects Greenlandic autonomy and culture — could bring transformative investment in infrastructure: modern ports, airports, telecommunications networks, hospitals, and educational institutions. Alaska's experience provides a useful model: following statehood, federal investment transformed Alaskan communities while preserving indigenous cultural heritage.

B. Tourism and Scientific Research

Greenland's dramatic landscapes — towering icebergs, vast fjords, the northern lights, and unique wildlife — have enormous ecotourism potential that remains largely untapped. Additionally, the island is a premier location for climate science, astronomy (due to minimal light pollution), and geological research. American stewardship could catalyze both industries, creating jobs and generating revenue.

C. The Alaska Dividend Model

Alaska's Permanent Fund, which distributes oil revenue dividends to every resident, demonstrates how resource wealth can be shared equitably. A similar model for Greenland could ensure that resource development benefits the Greenlandic people directly — not merely distant corporations or governments — creating a framework that is both economically productive and ethically sound.

V. Addressing Counterarguments

Any honest analysis must engage with the strongest objections to this proposal.

A. Sovereignty and Self-Determination

The most important objection concerns the rights of the Greenlandic people. Any acquisition must have the explicit, enthusiastic consent of Greenland's residents, expressed through a free and fair referendum. The United States should not — and morally cannot — impose sovereignty on an unwilling population. The argument presented here is not for coercion but for a compelling offer: a framework in which Greenlanders gain American citizenship, full representation in Congress, substantial federal investment, and a generous revenue-sharing arrangement, while retaining significant cultural autonomy — similar to the status of Native Alaskan communities or Pacific Island territories. Rare earths in particular are indispensable for advanced electronics, electric vehicles, wind turbines, defense systems, and precision-guided technologies. At present, global supply chains for many critical minerals are dangerously concentrated, with China dominating processing and, in some cases, production. That dependency creates serious vulnerabilities. A future in which the United States owns and develops Greenland’s mineral resources is one in which America gains leverage, resilience, and a stronger industrial base.

The energy potential of Greenland also deserves attention. Though development would need to be assessed carefully, Greenland may possess significant offshore oil and natural gas reserves. Even if some of these resources remain untapped for environmental or economic reasons, sovereign control over them would still carry strategic value. Ownership of major undeveloped reserves expands national options. It gives the United States flexibility in responding to future energy shortages, market shocks, or technological shifts. In an age when control over energy and critical resources remains central to global power, Greenland would function as a vast strategic reserve of future economic possibility.

Geography still matters profoundly in international politics. A United States that includes Greenland would possess a stronger territorial and maritime posture stretching across the northern hemisphere. It would gain greater influence over emerging Arctic shipping routes that could transform global trade patterns. As polar ice melt opens passages that shorten transit between Asia, Europe, and North America, countries that control key Arctic territories will shape the rules, security arrangements, and economic opportunities of this new maritime era. Denmark would receive substantial economic benefits and be relieved of the immense long-term burden of defending and administering a vast Arctic territory whose strategic significance increasingly exceeds Danish capacity. Meanwhile, Greenland itself could receive transformative investment in infrastructure, education, healthcare, and local economic development under an American framework. A carefully structured arrangement could benefit all parties while placing Greenland under the stewardship of the power best equipped to develop and defend it.

The purchase of Alaska was mocked as “Seward’s Folly,” only to prove one of the greatest bargains in history due to its strategic position and natural wealth.
